library(fpp3)

# How to use this deck

## Two parts

**Part 1: The big picture (plain language).**
What each idea *is*, why it exists, and how it connects to the models you already know. Almost no code or math.

**Part 2: Technical depth**
Same concepts as part 1 but with more technical details

# Part 1: The big picture

## Where we are

We have used three different ways for a model to "look at history":

| Way of seeing history | Examples |
|---|---|
| A **fixed window** of recent values | AR / ARIMA, NNAR |
| A **running memory** that gets updated | RNN, LSTM |
| **Selective lookback** that chooses which past moments matter | Attention, Transformers |

Here we add three families on top of that:

1. **Tree-based models** (random forests, gradient boosting) that learn from a *fixed window of lags* plus any other features you give them.
2. **Global models** that learn from *many series at once*.
3. **Attention**, the idea behind Transformers.

## Key Idea: forecasting as a table

A normal machine-learning model wants a **table**: one row per example, columns of inputs, and one column to predict.

A time series is not a table. But we can *make* it one:

| Row (day) | Demand yesterday | Demand 7 days ago | Temp yesterday | Day of week | **Demand today (target)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 210 | 205 | 25 | Mon | **224** |
| Tue | 224 | 211 | 29 | Tue | **231** |
| ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... |

- Each row says: "given what we knew *before* today, what happened today?"
- Once it is a table, **any** regression method can be used: linear regression, trees, neural nets.
- This is the same "lag" idea as an AR model, just not limited to straight lines.

## What is a decision tree?

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false}, 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    A{Is yesterday's demand above 230?} -->|Yes| B{Is today a weekend?}
    A -->|No| C{Was it hot yesterday?}
    B -->|Yes| D[Predict 225]
    B -->|No| E[Predict 250]
    C -->|Yes| F[Predict 238]
    C -->|No| G[Predict 205]
```

- The computer *learns* which questions to ask, and where to put the cut-offs, from past data.
- The final guess is simply the **average** of the past days that ended up in that box.
- A tree can capture curves, thresholds and "it depends" interactions that a straight-line model cannot.

## Why one tree is not enough

A single tree is easy to understand but jumpy: change the data a little and the questions change a lot.

Two fixes, both in plain language:

**Random forest: a committee.**
Train hundreds of trees, each on a slightly different random sample of the data and each allowed to ask only a random subset of questions. Then **average** them. Individual trees make different mistakes, and averaging cancels many of them out.

**Gradient boosting: a team of apprentices.**
Train a small tree. Look at what it got wrong. Train the next small tree **to fix those mistakes**. Repeat hundreds of times. The final forecast is the sum of everyone's corrections.

## Forest vs boosting, in one picture

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false}, 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif'}}}%%
flowchart TB
    subgraph Forest[Random forest: trees side by side]
    direction LR
    T1[Tree 1] --> AV[Average]
    T2[Tree 2] --> AV
    T3[Tree 3] --> AV
    end
    subgraph Boost[Boosting: trees in sequence]
    direction LR
    B1[Tree 1] -->|its mistakes| B2[Tree 2]
    B2 -->|remaining mistakes| B3[Tree 3]
    B3 --> SUM[Add corrections]
    end
```

- Forest: independent, then average. Reduces **variance**.
- Boosting: dependent, then add. Reduces **bias** step by step, so it needs more care not to overfit.

## What trees cannot do

A tree predicts by **averaging past values it has already seen**. So it can never predict a number outside the range of its training data, and it cannot keep following a trend.

If a series grows steadily, a tree trained on the early years will predict "about the largest thing I have seen" forever.

- ARIMA and ETS can continue a trend.
- Trees need help: model *changes* instead of *levels*, or combine them with a simple trend model.
- We will see this on real data in Part 2.

## What is a "global" model?

**Local model:** one model per series. 300 stores means 300 models, each learning only from its own short history.

**Global model:** *one* model trained on **all** the series together.

- Idea: many series share patterns (weekends, holidays, seasonality, recovery after a promotion).
- A short or noisy series can borrow strength from similar series.
- Series-specific information goes in as features (store type, region, the series' average size).
- This is the main reason machine learning has done well in large forecasting competitions.

## What is attention?

Imagine forecasting next week's sales. Not all past weeks matter equally: last week, the same week last year, and the last holiday matter more than a random Tuesday.

- An AR model gives each lag a **fixed** weight, always.
- An RNN/LSTM squeezes the whole past into one memory.
- **Attention** looks back over all past moments and assigns each a weight **that depends on the situation right now**, then takes the weighted average.

Think of searching a library: your question (the *query*) is compared with every book's label (the *key*), and you read mostly the books that match best (the *values*).

## The map

| Idea | One-line summary | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Lag features + trees | Turn the series into a table, learn rules | Many predictors, calendar effects, nonlinearity, moderate data |
| Random forest | Average many different trees | Robust default, little tuning |
| Gradient boosting | Trees that fix each other's mistakes | Usually the most accurate tabular method; needs tuning |
| Global model | One model for many series | Many related, short or noisy series |
| Attention / Transformers | Learned, situation-dependent lookback | Lots of data, long histories, many series |
| Classical (ETS / ARIMA) | A few parameters, built-in structure | One short series, trend extrapolation, need intervals |

The rest of the deck is about telling them apart.

## Self-check: Part 1

1. How do you turn a time series into a table, and what must be true of every input in a row?
2. What does a tree predict in a leaf, and why does that limit it?
3. Forest vs boosting: which reduces variance, which builds on mistakes?
4. What is the difference between a local and a global model?
5. How is attention different from the fixed lag weights of an AR model?

## Answers: Part 1

1. Each row has the target (today's value) and inputs like lags, rolling averages and calendar facts. Every input must be **known at the moment of forecasting**: nothing from after the time you are predicting.
2. The average of the training targets in that leaf. So predictions stay within the range of past values and cannot follow a trend beyond what was seen.
3. A forest averages independent trees (reducing variance). Boosting adds trees one after another, each correcting the previous ones' mistakes.
4. A local model is fit separately to each series. A global model is fit once on many series, with series-specific features.
5. AR uses the same weights every time. Attention computes weights from the current context, so which past moments matter changes with the situation.

# Part 2: Technical depth

# 2.1 Setting up the problem

## Forecasting as supervised learning

We want $\hat y_{t+h} = f(\mathbf{x}_t)$, where $\mathbf{x}_t$ is information available at time $t$:

$$
\mathbf{x}_t = (y_t, y_{t-1}, \dots, y_{t-p+1},\; \text{rolling statistics},\; \text{calendar features},\; \text{other series}).
$$

- Each time $t$ gives one **training example** $(\mathbf{x}_t, y_{t+h})$.
- With $f$ linear in $y_t,\dots,y_{t-p+1}$ this is an AR($p$) model fit by least squares.
- With $f$ a tree ensemble, $f$ can be nonlinear and can include interactions.
- No probability model for the errors is assumed, so **no automatic prediction intervals** (Section 2.9).

You now choose $p$, the features, the horizon strategy, and tuning parameters yourself.

## Known vs unknown inputs

At forecast time, features fall into three groups:

| Type | Example | Allowed at horizon $h$? |
|---|---|---|
| **Past values** | $y_{t-1}$, rolling mean of past days | Yes, if computed from data up to the forecast origin |
| **Known-in-advance** | Day of week, month, holiday, planned promotion | Yes, even for dates in the future |
| **Unknown future** | Tomorrow's temperature, tomorrow's sales of another product | **No**, unless you use a *forecast* of it |

Using tomorrow's actual temperature in an experiment overstates real-world accuracy. Our electricity example uses only *lagged* temperature for that reason.

## The data we will use

Daily electricity demand for Victoria, Australia (GWh), with maximum temperature and a holiday flag. The same data as in 11A.

```{r}
el <- vic_elec |>
  index_by(Date) |>
  summarise(Demand = sum(Demand) / 1000,
            Temp = max(Temperature),
            Holiday = as.numeric(any(Holiday))) |>
  as_tibble()

c(days = nrow(el), first = format(min(el$Date)), last = format(max(el$Date)))
```

- Train on 2012-2013, test on 2014, one step ahead, parameters fixed after training (the same design as 11A).

# 2.2 Feature engineering

## Building lag features

```{r}
feat <- el |>
  mutate(
    lag1 = lag(Demand, 1), lag2 = lag(Demand, 2), lag3 = lag(Demand, 3),
    lag7 = lag(Demand, 7), lag14 = lag(Demand, 14),
    roll7 = zoo::rollmeanr(lag(Demand, 1), 7, fill = NA),  # mean of the 7 days BEFORE today
    temp_l1 = lag(Temp, 1), temp_l2 = lag(Temp, 2),
    dow = lubridate::wday(Date), month = lubridate::month(Date)) |>
  filter(!is.na(lag14), !is.na(roll7))

train_end <- as.Date("2013-12-31")
tr <- feat |> filter(Date <= train_end)
te <- feat |> filter(Date >  train_end)
xs <- c("lag1", "lag2", "lag3", "lag7", "lag14", "roll7",
        "temp_l1", "temp_l2", "dow", "month", "Holiday")
c(train = nrow(tr), test = nrow(te), features = length(xs))
```

- `lag7` and `lag14` capture the weekly pattern; `roll7` smooths recent level.
- `lag()` shifts values *forward* in time, so each row only sees the past. `Holiday` and `dow` describe the day being forecast and are known in advance.

## Common feature ideas

| Feature family | Examples | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Lags | $y_{t-1},\ y_{t-7},\ y_{t-365}$ | Autocorrelation, seasonality |
| Rolling statistics | Mean, SD, min, max of the past $k$ values | Level and volatility |
| Differences / growth | $y_{t-1}-y_{t-2}$, percent change | Trend direction |
| Calendar | Day of week, month, holiday, days to holiday | Known seasonality |
| Fourier terms | $\sin(2\pi kt/m),\ \cos(2\pi kt/m)$ | Smooth seasonality with few columns |
| Other series | Lagged temperature, price, promotions | Drivers |

- Trees do **not** need features scaled or transformed monotonically.
- They *do* need you to supply the information: a tree cannot compute "demand 7 days ago" by itself.

## Data leakage

**Leakage** is any feature that contains information from the future of the row it describes. It makes experiments look great and real forecasts fail.

A typical mistake: a **centered** rolling mean, which averages days before *and after* today.

```{r}
leak <- el |>
  mutate(lag1 = lag(Demand, 1), lag7 = lag(Demand, 7), dow = lubridate::wday(Date),
         cent7 = zoo::rollmean(Demand, 7, fill = NA, align = "center")) |>
  filter(!is.na(lag7), !is.na(cent7))
trL <- leak |> filter(Date <= train_end); teL <- leak |> filter(Date > train_end)

fit_rmse <- function(cols) {
  m <- ranger(Demand ~ ., data = trL[, c("Demand", cols)], num.trees = 300, seed = 1)
  rmse(teL$Demand, predict(m, teL[, cols])$predictions)
}
c(lagged_only = fit_rmse(c("lag1", "lag7", "dow", "Holiday")),
  with_centered_mean = fit_rmse(c("lag1", "lag7", "dow", "Holiday", "cent7")))
```

The second number is better because the model is peeking at days after today. In real use that column would not exist.

## A leakage checklist

- Every rolling or lagged feature must use only rows **strictly before** the target date (use `lag()` first, then roll).
- Never compute scaling constants (means, SDs) or target-based encodings on the **whole** dataset; compute them on the training period only.
- Never shuffle rows before splitting (Section 2.6).
- For global models, cut **all** series at the same calendar date (Section 2.11).
- If results look too good, suspect leakage first.

# 2.3 Regression trees

## How a regression tree is built

Goal: split the feature space into regions $R_1,\dots,R_M$ and predict a constant $c_m$ in each:

$$
\hat f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} c_m \,\mathbf{1}\{\mathbf{x}\in R_m\},
\qquad c_m = \text{average of } y_i \text{ with } \mathbf{x}_i \in R_m.
$$

**Greedy recursive splitting.** At each node, try every feature $j$ and every threshold $s$, split into

$$
R_L(j,s)=\{\mathbf{x}: x_j \le s\}, \quad R_R(j,s)=\{\mathbf{x}: x_j > s\},
$$

and choose the pair that minimizes the total squared error

$$
\sum_{i\in R_L}(y_i-c_L)^2+\sum_{i\in R_R}(y_i-c_R)^2.
$$

Then repeat inside each child, until a stopping rule (maximum depth, minimum observations in a leaf).

## A small tree on the electricity data: the code

```{r}
#| output: false
small_tree <- rpart(Demand ~ temp_l1 + dow + Holiday + lag1, data = tr,
                    control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 3, cp = 0.001))
```

Four features, a maximum depth of 3.

## A small tree on the electricity data: the tree

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5
plot(small_tree, margin = 0.1, uniform = TRUE)
text(small_tree, use.n = TRUE, cex = 0.8)
```

- Each box is a question; each leaf shows the average demand (and the number of days) that landed there.
- `lag1` (yesterday's demand) usually enters first: the biggest reduction in squared error.

## Key properties of a tree

- **Piecewise constant:** the fitted function is a staircase. It can approximate any shape, but with enough data and splits.
- **Handles interactions automatically:** a split inside a split means "it depends on".
- **Invariant to monotone transformations** of a feature (only the order of values matters).
- **High variance:** small changes in data can change the first split and everything below it.
- **Depth controls complexity.** Deep trees fit noise; shallow trees underfit.
- **Bounded predictions:** a leaf value is an average of training targets, so $\min y_{\text{train}} \le \hat f \le \max y_{\text{train}}$. This is the root of the extrapolation problem (Section 2.8).

# 2.4 Random forests

## Bagging and the forest

**Bagging** (bootstrap aggregation): draw $B$ bootstrap samples of the rows, fit a deep tree to each, average the predictions:

$$
\hat f_{\text{bag}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac1B \sum_{b=1}^{B} \hat f_b(\mathbf{x}).
$$

**Random forest** adds one more idea: at each split, only a random subset of `mtry` features is considered. This *decorrelates* the trees.

If each tree has variance $\sigma^2$ and trees have pairwise correlation $\rho$:

$$
\operatorname{Var}\Big(\frac1B\sum_b \hat f_b\Big) = \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\,\sigma^2 .
$$

- More trees ($B\uparrow$) shrinks the second term only.
- Smaller `mtry` lowers $\rho$ (less correlated trees) but each tree is individually a bit worse.
- A forest does not overfit by adding more trees. How complex each tree is (its depth and leaf size) is covered in the next slides.

## Why more trees help: the second term

$$
\operatorname{Var}\Big(\frac1B\sum_b \hat f_b\Big) = \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\,\sigma^2
$$

- The **second term** is the part of each tree's noise that is unique to that tree. Averaging $B$ trees cancels it, at rate $1/B$.
- The **first term** is noise that all trees share (same data, same strong features). Averaging cannot cancel it.
- So adding trees helps quickly at first, then stops helping once the second term is small compared with $\rho\sigma^2$.

## Variance of the average as trees are added

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
expand.grid(B = 1:500, rho = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.6)) |>
  mutate(variance = rho + (1 - rho) / B, rho = factor(rho)) |>
  ggplot(aes(B, variance, colour = rho)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = as.numeric(as.character(rho)), colour = rho),
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of trees B (log scale)", y = "Variance of the average",
       colour = expression(rho))
```

Here $\sigma^2 = 1$. Each dashed line is the floor $\rho\sigma^2$ for the curve of the same color: the curve approaches it as $B$ grows but never goes below it. Lower correlation means a lower floor.

## Why a smaller `mtry` helps, and what it costs

At every split, a tree may only look at `mtry` randomly chosen features.

- **Benefit:** without the restriction, every tree opens with `lag1` (the strongest feature) and the trees come out nearly identical, so $\rho$ is high. Hiding some features forces trees to find different splits, so $\rho$ falls and the floor $\rho\sigma^2$ drops.
- **Cost:** a tree that is not allowed to see `lag1` at a split must use a weaker feature there. With a very small `mtry`, each tree is individually worse.
- The best `mtry` balances the two. We try it on electricity data, training through June 2013 and validating on July to December 2013 (the test year is not touched).

```{r}
fv_trn <- tr |> filter(Date <  as.Date("2013-07-01"))
fv_val <- tr |> filter(Date >= as.Date("2013-07-01"))

rf_fit <- function(...) ranger(Demand ~ ., data = fv_trn[, c("Demand", xs)], seed = 1, ...)
rf_err <- function(m) c(train = rmse(fv_trn$Demand, predict(m, fv_trn[, xs])$predictions),
                        validation = rmse(fv_val$Demand, predict(m, fv_val[, xs])$predictions))

sapply(c(1, 2, 4, 8, 11), function(k) round(rf_err(rf_fit(num.trees = 300, mtry = k)), 2)) |>
  `colnames<-`(paste0("mtry=", c(1, 2, 4, 8, 11)))
```

- With `mtry = 1` each tree is forced to split on one random feature at a time, and the forest is clearly worse.
- Past a few features there is little change: with 11 features, the extra choice at each split adds little here.

## What exactly are $\sigma^2$ and $\rho$?

Both are about the prediction at **one fixed input** $\mathbf{x}$ (say, a particular day), over the randomness in how the forest is built. They are not the variance or correlation of the demand data.

- **Randomness comes from two places:** which training data we happened to have, and the random choices inside the forest (bootstrap rows, `mtry` features).
- $\sigma^2$: how much one tree's prediction at $\mathbf{x}$ would vary if we rebuilt it from scratch.
- $\rho$: how strongly two different trees' predictions at $\mathbf{x}$ move together when we rebuild. Trees that read the same training data tend to be wrong in the same direction, which gives a positive $\rho$.
- Both are averaged over many points $\mathbf{x}$ in practice.

A common picture is that small `mtry` makes $\rho$ about 0 and large `mtry` makes $\rho$ about 1. That is not quite right. Trees in a forest are always built from the same data, so $\rho$ stays above 0. Reducing `mtry` lowers it. It does not reach 0, and a forest's $\rho$ is usually far from 1.

## Estimating $\sigma^2$ and $\rho$ in practice

You cannot read $\sigma^2$ and $\rho$ off a single fitted forest, because that forest has only one training set. The idea is to rebuild the forest on many resampled training sets:

1. Draw $K$ resampled training sets (here, 80% of the rows).
2. On each, fit a **1-tree** forest and a **$B$-tree** forest. Predict the validation days.
3. $\hat\sigma^2$ = the variance of the 1-tree predictions across the $K$ fits (at each day), averaged over days.
4. $V_B$ = the same quantity for the $B$-tree forest.
5. Solve the formula $V_B = \rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B$ for $\rho$.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
K <- 40; B <- 200
est_rho <- function(mtry) {
  P1 <- PB <- matrix(NA, nrow(fv_val), K)
  for (k in 1:K) {
    d <- fv_trn[sample(nrow(fv_trn), round(0.8 * nrow(fv_trn))), c("Demand", xs)]
    P1[, k] <- predict(ranger(Demand ~ ., d, num.trees = 1, mtry = mtry, seed = k), fv_val[, xs])$predictions
    PB[, k] <- predict(ranger(Demand ~ ., d, num.trees = B, mtry = mtry, seed = k), fv_val[, xs])$predictions
  }
  s2 <- mean(apply(P1, 1, var)); vB <- mean(apply(PB, 1, var))
  rho <- (vB - s2 / B) / (s2 - s2 / B)
  c(mtry = mtry, sigma2 = s2, var_forest = vB, rho = rho, floor = rho * s2)
}
round(t(sapply(c(1, 2, 4, 8, 11), est_rho)), 2)
```

## Reading the estimates

For comparison, the variance of the demand itself over the validation months is `r round(var(fv_val$Demand))`.

- **$\sigma^2$ is large.** One tree is very unstable (its variance is a large fraction of the variance of demand), and a forest of $B$ trees is far more stable.
- **$\rho$ is small, but it is the floor $\rho\sigma^2$ that matters.** A small correlation times a large $\sigma^2$ is what stays after averaging many trees.
- **As `mtry` increases, $\rho$ rises and $\sigma^2$ falls.** Trees that see more features are more alike (higher $\rho$), but each one is more stable (lower $\sigma^2$).
- **Variance is only half of the story.** The floor is smallest at `mtry = 1`, yet that setting has the worst validation error on the previous slide. Hiding features lowers variance and raises each tree's bias.
- The resampled sets share 80% of their rows and the rows are autocorrelated, so this understates the true variation from new data. Treat these as rough estimates of scale, not exact values.

## What is the depth of a tree?

**Depth** is the number of questions in a row from the top of the tree down to a leaf.

The demand tree from earlier has depth 2: first "is yesterday's demand above 230?", then one more question, then a prediction.

| Depth | Maximum number of leaves | What the tree looks like |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | One question. Two broad groups of days |
| 2 | 4 | Two questions in a row |
| 3 | 8 | Starts to separate special cases |
| 5 | 32 | Many small groups |
| 10 | 1,024 | Each group may hold only a handful of days |

- Each extra level can double the number of leaves.
- A **shallow** tree makes a few coarse groups and misses detail (underfit).
- A **deep** tree makes many tiny groups, and starts fitting the noise in individual days (overfit).

## What is leaf size?

**Leaf size** is how many training days land in a leaf (a final box). The prediction for the leaf is the average of those days.

- Leaf size 1: the box holds one day, the prediction is that day's value, and the training error is exactly zero. The tree has memorized the data.
- Leaf size 50: the prediction averages 50 days, so one unusual day barely matters.
- In `ranger`, `min.node.size` sets the size below which a box is not split further. In `rpart` the corresponding setting is `minbucket`.

Depth and leaf size are two ways to limit the same thing: **how finely the tree chops up the data**. Deep trees and small leaves both give many small groups.

## Overfitting a single tree: the code

Fit single trees to the same training period and score them on the validation months, varying depth and leaf size.

```{r}
#| output: false
tree_err <- function(depth = 30, leaf = 1) {
  m <- rpart(Demand ~ ., data = fv_trn[, c("Demand", xs)],
             control = rpart.control(maxdepth = depth, cp = 0, minsplit = 2, minbucket = leaf))
  c(train = rmse(fv_trn$Demand, predict(m, fv_trn)),
    validation = rmse(fv_val$Demand, predict(m, fv_val)))
}
by_depth <- sapply(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12), function(d) tree_err(depth = d))
by_leaf  <- sapply(c(1, 3, 10, 30, 60),     function(k) tree_err(leaf = k))

p_single <- bind_rows(
  tibble(setting = "Depth (leaf size 1)", value = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12), as_tibble(t(by_depth))),
  tibble(setting = "Minimum leaf size (no depth limit)", value = c(1, 3, 10, 30, 60), as_tibble(t(by_leaf)))) |>
  pivot_longer(c(train, validation), names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, rmse, colour = set)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~setting, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "RMSE", colour = NULL)
```

## Overfitting a single tree: the result

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_single
```

- Training error always falls as the tree gets more flexible. It reaches zero with leaf size 1.
- Validation error is best at a moderate depth or leaf size, then rises: the tree is fitting noise.

## Forests are more forgiving: the code

Same experiment on a forest of 300 trees (`mtry = 4`). `max.depth` limits depth and `min.node.size` sets leaf size.

```{r}
#| output: false
depths <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20); leaves <- c(1, 5, 20, 50, 100)
f_depth <- sapply(depths, function(d) rf_err(rf_fit(num.trees = 300, mtry = 4, max.depth = d)))
f_leaf  <- sapply(leaves, function(k) rf_err(rf_fit(num.trees = 300, mtry = 4, min.node.size = k)))

p_forest <- bind_rows(
  tibble(setting = "Maximum depth", value = depths, as_tibble(t(f_depth))),
  tibble(setting = "Minimum leaf size", value = leaves, as_tibble(t(f_leaf)))) |>
  pivot_longer(c(train, validation), names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, rmse, colour = set)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~setting, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "RMSE", colour = NULL)
```

## Forests are more forgiving: the result

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_forest
```

- Validation error does **not** rise for deep trees or small leaves. Averaging many deep trees cancels most of the noise each one fits.
- Forests go wrong by being **restricted too much**: very shallow trees or very large leaves underfit.

## Forests are more forgiving: what to take

- The training curve is in-sample, so use the validation curve.
- A forest defaults to deep trees with small leaves, while a single tree needs depth or leaf size controlled.

## Fitting a forest on the electricity data

```{r}
rf <- ranger(Demand ~ ., data = tr[, c("Demand", xs)],
             num.trees = 500, mtry = 4, min.node.size = 5, seed = 1)
rf_pred <- predict(rf, te[, xs])$predictions

c(RMSE_test = rmse(te$Demand, rf_pred), OOB_RMSE_train = sqrt(rf$prediction.error))
```

- `num.trees`, `mtry`, `min.node.size` are the main settings. Defaults are usually decent.
- **OOB (out-of-bag) error:** each tree leaves out about a third of rows; predicting those rows from the trees that did not see them gives a free error estimate.

::: {.callout-warning}
OOB estimates assume rows are exchangeable. In a lag table neighbouring rows share nearly identical features, so OOB is usually **optimistic** for time series. Above, the OOB RMSE (about 12) is well below the true out-of-sample RMSE on 2014 (about 16); part of that gap is that 2014 is simply a different year, but this is exactly the pattern to expect. Use time-ordered validation instead.
:::

# 2.5 Gradient boosting

## The boosting idea, formally

Build an additive model, one small tree at a time:

$$
F_0(\mathbf{x}) = \bar y, \qquad F_m(\mathbf{x}) = F_{m-1}(\mathbf{x}) + \eta\, h_m(\mathbf{x}),
$$

where $h_m$ is a small tree fit to the **negative gradient** of the loss at the current predictions, and $\eta\in(0,1]$ is the **learning rate** (shrinkage).

For squared-error loss $L=\tfrac12(y-F)^2$, the negative gradient is just the **residual** $y-F_{m-1}(\mathbf{x})$. So:

1. Compute residuals of the current model.
2. Fit a small tree to the residuals.
3. Add a fraction $\eta$ of it to the model.
4. Repeat for $M$ rounds.

Small $\eta$ with many rounds generally generalizes better than large $\eta$ with few rounds.

## Boosting by hand: a minimal implementation

```{r}
boost_by_hand <- function(X, y, rounds = 200, eta = 0.1, depth = 2) {
  F <- rep(mean(y), length(y)); trees <- vector("list", rounds)
  d <- data.frame(X)
  for (m in seq_len(rounds)) {
    d$r <- y - F                                  # residuals = negative gradient
    trees[[m]] <- rpart(r ~ ., data = d, control = rpart.control(maxdepth = depth, cp = 0))
    F <- F + eta * predict(trees[[m]], d)         # take a small step
  }
  list(base = mean(y), trees = trees, eta = eta)
}
predict_by_hand <- function(fit, X) {
  d <- data.frame(X)
  fit$base + fit$eta * Reduce(`+`, lapply(fit$trees, predict, newdata = d))
}
bh <- boost_by_hand(tr[, xs], tr$Demand)
rmse(te$Demand, predict_by_hand(bh, te[, xs]))
```

About fifteen lines is the whole algorithm, and its test RMSE is in the same range as the XGBoost fit on the next slides. XGBoost is a very fast, regularized, carefully engineered version of exactly this loop.

## What XGBoost adds: the objective

$$
L = \sum_i \ell(y_i,\hat y_i) + \sum_k \Omega(f_k)
$$

- $\ell(y_i,\hat y_i)$ is the loss for one row, for example $(y_i-\hat y_i)^2$. The first sum is over rows.
- $k$ indexes the **trees**: $\hat y_i = f_1(\mathbf{x}_i)+\dots+f_K(\mathbf{x}_i)$. Each tree pays $\Omega(f)=\gamma T+\tfrac12\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$, with $T$ leaves and leaf values $\mathbf{w}$.
- $w_j$ is the number a tree outputs in leaf $j$. It plays the role of $c_m$ in a single regression tree, but it is a **correction** to the current prediction, not the average of $y$.

## What XGBoost adds: the parabola

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
s0 <- 0.5                                       # current score for a row with y = 1 (log-loss)
p0 <- 1 / (1 + exp(-s0)); g0 <- p0 - 1; h0 <- p0 * (1 - p0)
l0 <- log(1 + exp(-s0))
tibble(w = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 200)) |>
  mutate(`actual loss` = log(1 + exp(-(s0 + w))),
         `parabola (slope g, curvature h)` = l0 + g0 * w + 0.5 * h0 * w^2) |>
  pivot_longer(-w, names_to = "curve", values_to = "loss") |>
  ggplot(aes(w, loss, colour = curve)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 3.5)) +
  labs(x = "Change w added to this row's prediction", y = "Loss for this row", colour = NULL)
```

The loss for one row, as a function of the change $w$ we add to its prediction. Near $w=0$ a parabola fits it closely. For squared error the loss is exactly a parabola.

## What XGBoost adds: the leaf value

Near the current prediction, one row's loss is approximately a parabola in the change $w$:

$$
\ell(y_i,\hat y_i+w) \approx \ell(y_i,\hat y_i) + g_i\,w + \tfrac12 h_i\,w^2
$$

- $g_i$ is the slope and $h_i$ the curvature (squared error: $g_i=\hat y_i-y_i$, $h_i=1$).
- For a leaf, add over its rows and add the penalty $\tfrac12\lambda w^2$: $G\,w + \tfrac12(H+\lambda)\,w^2$, with $G=\sum g_i$, $H=\sum h_i$.
- The lowest point of that parabola is $w^{*} = -G/(H+\lambda)$.

## What XGBoost adds: the split gain

The **gain** of splitting a node into left and right children is

$$
\text{Gain}=\tfrac12\Big[\tfrac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda}+\tfrac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda}-\tfrac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda}\Big]-\gamma .
$$

A split is kept only if the gain is positive, so $\gamma$ and $\lambda$ directly control overfitting.

## XGBoost by hand: $g$ and $h$

```{r}
xd <- data.frame(temp = c(31, 18, 36, 22, 27, 15, 38, 24),
                 y    = c(44, 22, 47, 25, 38, 20, 42, 29))
lambda <- 1                    # leaf penalty
F0 <- mean(xd$y)               # starting prediction
xd$g <- F0 - xd$y              # slope of the loss
xd$h <- 1                      # curvature of the loss
t(xd)
```

- `temp`: yesterday's maximum temperature. `y`: today's demand. Starting prediction $\hat y = `r F0`$ (the mean of $y$) for every row.
- $g_i = \hat y_i - y_i$ is the negative residual, and $h_i = 1$.

## XGBoost by hand: leaf values

```{r}
leaf_stats <- function(rows) {
  G <- sum(xd$g[rows]); H <- sum(xd$h[rows])
  c(G = G, H = H, w = -G / (H + lambda), avg_residual = -G / H)
}
left <- xd$temp <= 24
rbind(left = leaf_stats(left), right = leaf_stats(!left))
```

- Split at `temp <= 24`. Each leaf sums $g_i$ and $h_i$ over its rows, and $w^* = -G/(H+\lambda)$.
- With $\lambda = 0$, $w^*$ is the average residual (last column).
- With $\lambda = `r lambda`$ the left leaf moves from `r round(leaf_stats(left)["avg_residual"], 2)` to `r round(leaf_stats(left)["w"], 2)`.

## XGBoost by hand: choosing the split

Score every split with the gain formula. The best split has the largest gain.

```{r}
cuts <- sort(xd$temp)[-nrow(xd)]     # candidate splits
gain <- function(s) {
  L <- xd$temp <= s
  GL <- sum(xd$g[L]);  HL <- sum(xd$h[L])
  GR <- sum(xd$g[!L]); HR <- sum(xd$h[!L])
  0.5 * (GL^2 / (HL + lambda) + GR^2 / (HR + lambda) -
         (GL + GR)^2 / (HL + HR + lambda))
}
round(setNames(sapply(cuts, gain), paste0("temp<=", cuts)), 1)
```

- The split at `temp <= 24` has the largest gain. `xgboost` reports gain without the $\tfrac12$, so its number is twice ours.

## XGBoost by hand: the check

```{r}
w_left <- leaf_stats(left)["w"]; w_right <- leaf_stats(!left)["w"]
xg1 <- xgb.train(
  params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = 1, max_depth = 1,
                lambda = lambda, min_child_weight = 0, base_score = F0),
  data = xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(xd["temp"]), label = xd$y),
  nrounds = 1, verbose = 0)
X1 <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(xd["temp"]))
rbind(by_hand = F0 + ifelse(left, w_left, w_right),
      xgboost = predict(xg1, X1))
```

- One round with `eta = 1` gives the same predictions as our hand calculation.
- `xgboost` writes the same split as `temp < 27`, which separates the same days.

## Why curvature helps

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
tibble(p = seq(0, 1, length.out = 101)) |>
  mutate(`squared error` = 1, `log-loss (classification)` = p * (1 - p)) |>
  pivot_longer(-p, names_to = "loss", values_to = "h") |>
  ggplot(aes(p, h, colour = loss)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Predicted probability p (log-loss only)", y = "Curvature h", colour = NULL)
```

## Why curvature helps: what changes

- **Squared error:** $h_i = 1$ for every row, so $H$ just counts rows and $w^*$ is the average residual, shrunk by $\lambda$. Curvature adds nothing beyond plain boosting.
- **Log-loss:** $g_i = p_i - y_i$ and $h_i = p_i(1-p_i)$. A row the model is already sure of ($p$ near 0 or 1) has $h$ near 0 and little say in the leaf. A row at $p = 0.5$ has the most.
- $H$ sits in the denominator of $w^*$, so the step size adapts to how confident the model is. This is where second-order matters: classification, counts and quantile losses.

## The main boosting settings

| Setting (xgboost name) | Effect |
|---|---|
| `nrounds` | Number of trees. More rounds fit more; choose with validation |
| `eta` | Learning rate. Smaller is safer and needs more rounds |
| `max_depth` | Depth of each tree. 3 to 6 typical; controls interaction order |
| `subsample` | Fraction of rows per tree. Below 1 adds randomness and reduces overfitting |
| `colsample_bytree` | Fraction of features per tree |
| `min_child_weight` | Minimum curvature sum in a leaf. Larger is more conservative |
| `lambda`, `gamma` | L2 penalty on leaf weights, minimum gain to split |

For time series, the **number of rounds** is usually chosen by early stopping on a *later* validation period.

## Fitting XGBoost

```{r}
dtr <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(tr[, xs]), label = tr$Demand)
dte <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(te[, xs]), label = te$Demand)

xg <- xgb.train(
  params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = 0.05, max_depth = 4,
                subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8),
  data = dtr, nrounds = 300, verbose = 0)

rmse(te$Demand, predict(xg, dte))
```

## Watching overfitting: the code

```{r}
#| output: false
curve_fit <- xgb.train(
  params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = 0.05, max_depth = 6,
                subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8),
  data = dtr, nrounds = 600, evals = list(train = dtr, test = dte), verbose = 0)

p_curve <- as_tibble(attributes(curve_fit)$evaluation_log) |>
  pivot_longer(-iter, names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(iter, rmse, colour = set)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Boosting rounds", y = "RMSE", colour = NULL)
```

- The test set is used only to draw this picture. To choose `nrounds`, use a separate validation period (below).

## Watching overfitting: the learning curve

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_curve
```

- Training error keeps falling. Test error stops improving, and may rise.
- Training error is *not* a guide to forecast accuracy.

# 2.6 Validation and tuning for time series

## Why shuffled cross-validation is wrong

Standard $k$-fold CV shuffles rows. For time series that means:

- Training rows from the **future** of a test row. The model "knows" what happens next.
- Neighbouring rows (nearly identical lag features) split across train and test.

The correct scheme is **time-ordered**: always train on the past, test on the future (rolling-origin / expanding-window CV).

## Time-ordered folds

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.8
tibble(fold = rep(1:3, each = 12), t = rep(1:12, 3),
       role = c(rep(c("train", "test", "unused"), c(3, 3, 6)),
                rep(c("train", "test", "unused"), c(6, 3, 3)),
                rep(c("train", "test", "unused"), c(9, 3, 0)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(t, factor(fold), fill = role)) + geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(train = "#2a78d6", test = "#eb6834", unused = "grey90")) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Fold", fill = NULL)
```

Each fold trains on the past and tests on the block that follows.

## Shuffled vs time-ordered CV on our data

```{r}
all_rows <- feat
fit_eval <- function(trn, tst) {
  m <- ranger(Demand ~ ., data = all_rows[trn, c("Demand", xs)], num.trees = 300, seed = 1)
  rmse(all_rows$Demand[tst], predict(m, all_rows[tst, xs])$predictions)
}

set.seed(2)
fold_id <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(all_rows)))
shuffled <- sapply(1:5, function(k) fit_eval(which(fold_id != k), which(fold_id == k)))

idx <- which(all_rows$Date > as.Date("2013-01-01"))
blocks <- split(idx, cut(seq_along(idx), 5, labels = FALSE))
ordered <- sapply(blocks, function(b) fit_eval(1:(min(b) - 1), b))

rbind(shuffled = round(shuffled, 2), time_ordered = round(ordered, 2))
c(shuffled_mean = mean(shuffled), time_ordered_mean = mean(ordered))
```

- Here the average gap is modest, but the **time-ordered folds vary a lot** (some blocks are much harder, e.g. summer peaks). Shuffled folds hide that.
- A single test period (like 2014) is one draw from this variation. Treat any single split with caution.

## Setting up the tuning

We choose `max_depth` and the number of rounds.

- **Validation blocks:** the last three quarters of the training period. Train on the days before a block, score on the block.
- **Why also hold out a test year:** the best validation score is optimistic, because many candidates were compared on it. The test year is used once, after all choices are made.
- **How we choose:** the minimum validation RMSE, for ease of coding. If the curve is flat near the minimum, the elbow or the simplest setting within one standard error is a common alternative.

## Tuning with time-ordered folds

We choose `max_depth` and the number of rounds using three validation blocks at the end of the **training** period only.

```{r}
val_blocks <- list(c("2013-04-01", "2013-06-30"),
                   c("2013-07-01", "2013-09-30"),
                   c("2013-10-01", "2013-12-31"))

tune_one <- function(depth, eta = 0.05, max_rounds = 400) {
  logs <- sapply(val_blocks, function(b) {
    s <- as.Date(b[1]); e <- as.Date(b[2])
    trn <- tr |> filter(Date < s); val <- tr |> filter(Date >= s, Date <= e)
    d1 <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(trn[, xs]), label = trn$Demand)
    d2 <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(val[, xs]), label = val$Demand)
    f <- xgb.train(params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = eta, max_depth = depth,
                                 subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8),
                   data = d1, nrounds = max_rounds, evals = list(val = d2), verbose = 0)
    attributes(f)$evaluation_log$val_rmse
  })
  mean_curve <- rowMeans(logs)
  tibble(depth = depth, best_rounds = which.min(mean_curve), cv_rmse = min(mean_curve))
}
tuning <- bind_rows(lapply(c(2, 3, 4, 6), tune_one))
tuning
```

## Using the tuned settings

```{r}
best <- tuning |> slice_min(cv_rmse, n = 1)
best

xg_tuned <- xgb.train(
  params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = 0.05, max_depth = best$depth,
                subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8),
  data = dtr, nrounds = best$best_rounds, verbose = 0)

c(untuned_test = rmse(te$Demand, predict(xg, dte)),
  tuned_test   = rmse(te$Demand, predict(xg_tuned, dte)))
```

- The test set was touched only once, after all choices were made.
- Notice the tuned model is **not better** on the test year than the untuned one. The validation blocks (three quarters of 2013) gave RMSE near 8, while the test year gives about 15: different periods have different difficulty, so tuning gains on one period need not carry over. Tuning is worth doing, but expect modest, noisy gains.
- Tuning on the test set is the most common way to fool yourself.

# 2.7 Results on the electricity data

## Trees vs classical models

Classical models for the same task: ETS, ARIMA, and a lag regression with ARIMA errors given the same calendar information (day-of-week and holiday), all fixed after training and scored one step ahead.

```{r}
el_ts <- el |>
  mutate(Temp2 = Temp^2, T_l1 = lag(Temp, 1), T2_l1 = lag(Temp2, 1),
         dow2 = as.numeric(lubridate::wday(Date) == 2), dow3 = as.numeric(lubridate::wday(Date) == 3),
         dow4 = as.numeric(lubridate::wday(Date) == 4), dow5 = as.numeric(lubridate::wday(Date) == 5),
         dow6 = as.numeric(lubridate::wday(Date) == 6), dow7 = as.numeric(lubridate::wday(Date) == 7)) |>
  filter(!is.na(T_l1)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Date)

fits <- el_ts |> filter(Date <= train_end) |>
  model(SNAIVE = SNAIVE(Demand),
        ETS    = ETS(Demand),
        ARIMA  = ARIMA(Demand),
        LagReg = ARIMA(Demand ~ T_l1 + T2_l1 + Holiday + dow2 + dow3 + dow4 + dow5 + dow6 + dow7))

classical <- refit(fits, el_ts, reestimate = FALSE) |>
  augment() |> as_tibble() |> filter(Date > train_end) |>
  group_by(model = .model) |> summarise(RMSE = rmse(Demand, .fitted))
```

## The scoreboard

```{r}
ml <- tibble(model = c("Random forest", "XGBoost (untuned)", "XGBoost (tuned)"),
             RMSE = c(rmse(te$Demand, rf_pred),
                      rmse(te$Demand, predict(xg, dte)),
                      rmse(te$Demand, predict(xg_tuned, dte))))
bind_rows(classical, ml) |>
  mutate(`vs seasonal naive` = RMSE / RMSE[model == "SNAIVE"]) |>
  arrange(RMSE) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

## How to read this table

- All of these learn the strong weekly and calendar structure, so every model is far better than seasonal naive.
- **The trees are not automatically better than the classical models.** XGBoost beat plain ARIMA, but ETS and the lag regression (given the same calendar information) were both better, and the random forest was about level with ARIMA.
- One year, one split, one step ahead: the ranking among the close models is not reliable.
- Where trees *should* help: many predictors, nonlinear effects and interactions that you did not specify (they find the U-shape in temperature by themselves), and very many series (Section 2.11).
- Where they struggle: trends (next section).

# 2.8 Trees and trends

## The extrapolation problem, on real data

Quarterly Australian electricity production has a strong upward trend. Train through 1995, then test 1996-2010.

```{r}
ap <- aus_production |>
  transmute(Quarter, y = Electricity) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(l1 = lag(y, 1), l2 = lag(y, 2), l3 = lag(y, 3), l4 = lag(y, 4),
         q = lubridate::quarter(Quarter)) |>
  filter(!is.na(l4))
ap_tr <- ap |> filter(Quarter <= yearquarter("1995 Q4"))
ap_te <- ap |> filter(Quarter >  yearquarter("1995 Q4"))
lag_cols <- c("l1", "l2", "l3", "l4", "q")

c(train_max = max(ap_tr$y), test_max = max(ap_te$y))
```

The test period contains values far above anything in training.

## One-step forecasts: the code

```{r}
#| output: false
ap_rf <- ranger(y ~ ., data = ap_tr[, c("y", lag_cols)], num.trees = 500, seed = 1)
ap_xg <- xgb.train(params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = 0.05, max_depth = 3),
                   data = xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(ap_tr[, lag_cols]), label = ap_tr$y),
                   nrounds = 300, verbose = 0)

ap_res <- ap_te |> mutate(
  RF  = predict(ap_rf, ap_te[, lag_cols])$predictions,
  XGB = predict(ap_xg, xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(ap_te[, lag_cols]))))

p_trend <- ap_res |> rename(Actual = y) |> pivot_longer(c(Actual, RF, XGB)) |>
  ggplot(aes(as.Date(Quarter), value, colour = name)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Electricity", colour = NULL)
```

## One-step forecasts: the result

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_trend
```

- Both tree models flatten out near the largest training value while the series keeps climbing.

## Fix 1: model changes, not levels

Predict the *change from the same quarter last year*, $y_t-y_{t-4}$, then add it back. The target now stays within the range seen in training.

```{r}
ap_tr2 <- ap_tr |> mutate(d = y - l4)
ap_rf_d <- ranger(d ~ ., data = ap_tr2[, c("d", lag_cols)], num.trees = 500, seed = 1)
ap_diff_pred <- ap_te$l4 + predict(ap_rf_d, ap_te[, lag_cols])$predictions

ap_classical <- {
  f <- aus_production |> filter(Quarter <= yearquarter("1995 Q4")) |>
    model(ETS = ETS(Electricity), ARIMA = ARIMA(Electricity), SNAIVE = SNAIVE(Electricity))
  refit(f, aus_production, reestimate = FALSE) |> augment() |> as_tibble() |>
    filter(Quarter > yearquarter("1995 Q4")) |>
    group_by(model = .model) |> summarise(RMSE = rmse(Electricity, .fitted))
}

bind_rows(
  ap_classical,
  tibble(model = c("RF on levels", "XGBoost on levels", "RF on seasonal difference"),
         RMSE = c(rmse(ap_te$y, ap_res$RF), rmse(ap_te$y, ap_res$XGB),
                  rmse(ap_te$y, ap_diff_pred)))) |>
  arrange(RMSE) |> mutate(RMSE = round(RMSE))
```

## Other ways to handle trends

- **Difference or take growth rates** before modelling (as above), then add the level back. Often the first thing to try.
- **Hybrid:** fit a simple trend (linear regression or ETS), then fit trees to the **residuals**. The trend model extrapolates; the trees capture what is left.
- **Include a linear model inside the leaves** (model trees, or LightGBM's `linear_tree` option), so each region has its own slope.
- **Normalize each series by a recent level** (global models do this routinely).
- Or use a model that extrapolates by design (ETS, ARIMA with drift) and give the trees the *exogenous* features.

# 2.9 Multi-step forecasts and uncertainty

## Three ways to forecast $h$ steps ahead

| Strategy | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Recursive** | One one-step model. Forecast $\hat y_{t+1}$, feed it back as a lag, repeat | One model; uses all data | Errors compound; needs forecasts of any other inputs |
| **Direct** | A separate model for each horizon $h$ (target $y_{t+h}$, features at $t$) | No compounding; each model targets its own horizon | $H$ models; ignores relationships between horizons |
| **Multi-output** | One model predicts all $H$ values together (natural for neural nets) | Shares structure across horizons | Needs a model that supports vector targets |

Classical models (ARIMA, ETS) are recursive by construction.

## Direct vs recursive: sunspots, 10 steps ahead

Square-root sunspot counts, 9 lags, XGBoost. Train through 1958, forecast from every origin 1958 to 1978.

```{r}
y <- as.numeric(sqrt(sunspot.year)); n <- length(y); p <- 9; H <- 10
T0 <- which(as.numeric(time(sunspot.year)) == 1958)

make_xy <- function(y, p, h) {
  t_idx <- p:(length(y) - h)
  X <- t(sapply(t_idx, function(t) y[t:(t - p + 1)])); colnames(X) <- paste0("l", 0:(p - 1))
  list(X = X, y = y[t_idx + h])
}
fit_xgb <- function(X, y) xgb.train(
  params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = 0.05, max_depth = 3, subsample = 0.8),
  data = xgb.DMatrix(X, label = y), nrounds = 200, verbose = 0)

ytr <- y[1:T0]
direct_models <- lapply(1:H, function(h) { d <- make_xy(ytr, p, h); fit_xgb(d$X, d$y) })
one_step <- { d <- make_xy(ytr, p, 1); fit_xgb(d$X, d$y) }
```

## Running both strategies

```{r}
as_row <- function(v) { m <- matrix(v, nrow = 1); colnames(m) <- paste0("l", 0:(p - 1)); xgb.DMatrix(m) }

errs <- lapply(T0:(n - H), function(o) {
  buf <- y[1:o]; rec <- numeric(H)
  for (h in 1:H) { rec[h] <- predict(one_step, as_row(rev(tail(buf, p)))); buf <- c(buf, rec[h]) }
  x <- as_row(rev(tail(y[1:o], p)))
  tibble(h = 1:H, actual = y[o + 1:H], recursive = rec,
         direct = sapply(1:H, function(k) predict(direct_models[[k]], x)),
         naive = y[o])
}) |> bind_rows()

errs |> group_by(h) |>
  summarise(across(c(recursive, direct, naive), ~ rmse(actual, .x))) |>
  mutate(across(-h, ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

- Neither strategy wins at every horizon; the leader flips from one horizon to the next. The differences are within noise.
- Both beat the naive forecast by a wide margin at medium horizons; by horizon 10 all three are similar.
- Few origins and one series: treat this as an illustration of the mechanics, not a verdict on the strategies.

## Prediction intervals for tree models

Trees give point forecasts. Intervals need an extra step. Three practical options:

1. **Quantile regression forests:** each leaf stores *all* training targets (not only the average); the forecast distribution is the weighted empirical distribution of those values. In `ranger`, set `quantreg = TRUE`.
2. **Quantile boosting:** train with a quantile loss ("pinball loss") for each quantile you want (for example the 5% and 95% quantiles).
3. **Conformal prediction:** use the model's errors on a held-out calibration period to size the interval: $\hat y \pm q$, where $q$ is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of absolute calibration errors.

## Quantile forest on electricity

```{r}
rq <- ranger(Demand ~ ., data = tr[, c("Demand", xs)], num.trees = 500,
             quantreg = TRUE, seed = 1)
qs <- predict(rq, te[, xs], type = "quantiles", quantiles = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))$predictions

c(coverage_90 = mean(te$Demand >= qs[, 1] & te$Demand <= qs[, 3]),
  avg_width = mean(qs[, 3] - qs[, 1]))
```

- Empirical coverage near the nominal 90% is the target. Always check it on held-out data.
- Intervals rely on future errors resembling past errors; they will be too narrow if conditions change.

## Quantile forest: the intervals

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
tibble(Date = te$Date, actual = te$Demand, lo = qs[, 1], mid = qs[, 2], hi = qs[, 3]) |>
  filter(Date < as.Date("2014-03-01")) |>
  ggplot(aes(Date)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mid), colour = "#2a78d6") + geom_line(aes(y = actual)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Demand (GWh)", title = "90% interval (blue band), actual (black), one step ahead")
```

## Quantile boosting on electricity

```{r}
qb <- xgb.train(
  params = list(objective = "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95),
                eta = 0.05, max_depth = 4, subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8, seed = 1),
  data = dtr, nrounds = 300, verbose = 0)
qb_pred <- predict(qb, xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(te[, xs])))

qb_cov <- mean(te$Demand >= qb_pred[, 1] & te$Demand <= qb_pred[, 3])
c(coverage_90 = qb_cov, avg_width = mean(qb_pred[, 3] - qb_pred[, 1]))
```

- One model, trained with the pinball loss, returns the 5%, 50% and 95% quantiles.
- Coverage on 2014 is `r round(100 * qb_cov)`%, against a 90% target.

## Quantile boosting: the intervals

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
tibble(Date = te$Date, actual = te$Demand, lo = qb_pred[, 1], mid = qb_pred[, 2], hi = qb_pred[, 3]) |>
  filter(Date < as.Date("2014-03-01")) |>
  ggplot(aes(Date)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mid), colour = "#2a78d6") + geom_line(aes(y = actual)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Demand (GWh)", title = "90% interval (blue band), actual (black), one step ahead")
```

## Conformal prediction on electricity

```{r}
alpha <- 0.1
cp_model <- xgb.train(
  params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = 0.05, max_depth = 4,
                subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8, seed = 1),
  data = xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(fv_trn[, xs]), label = fv_trn$Demand), nrounds = 300, verbose = 0)
cal_err <- abs(fv_val$Demand - predict(cp_model, xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(fv_val[, xs]))))
n_cal <- length(cal_err)
q_hat <- quantile(cal_err, ceiling((n_cal + 1) * (1 - alpha)) / n_cal)
cp_pred <- predict(cp_model, xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(te[, xs])))
cp_cov <- mean(abs(te$Demand - cp_pred) <= q_hat)
c(q_hat = unname(q_hat), coverage_90 = cp_cov, avg_width = 2 * unname(q_hat))
```

- Calibration set: errors on July to December 2013. $\hat q$ is their 90% quantile, and the interval is the forecast $\pm\,\hat q$. Coverage on 2014 is `r round(100 * cp_cov)`%.

## Conformal prediction: the intervals

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
tibble(Date = te$Date, actual = te$Demand, pred = cp_pred, lo = cp_pred - q_hat, hi = cp_pred + q_hat) |>
  filter(Date < as.Date("2014-03-01")) |>
  ggplot(aes(Date)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred), colour = "#2a78d6") + geom_line(aes(y = actual)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Demand (GWh)", title = "90% interval (blue band), actual (black), one step ahead")
```

# 2.10 Interpretation

## What did the model learn?

**Permutation importance:** the rise in error when one feature is scrambled.

1. Compute the model's error (MSE) on the data as it is.
2. **Shuffle one feature:** reorder that column's values at random among the rows. Other columns and the target stay put, so each row gets another row's value for this feature.
3. Recompute the error. Importance is the **increase** in MSE. Repeat for each feature.
4. A big increase means the model relied on the feature. Near zero means it did not.

## Permutation importance: the code

```{r}
#| output: false
rfi <- ranger(Demand ~ ., data = tr[, c("Demand", xs)], num.trees = 500,
              importance = "permutation", seed = 1)
p_imp <- tibble(feature = names(rfi$variable.importance), importance = rfi$variable.importance) |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(feature, importance), importance)) + geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  coord_flip() + labs(x = NULL, y = "Increase in MSE when shuffled")
```

## Permutation importance: the result

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_imp
```

- Recent demand and the weekly pattern matter most.
- **Caution:** correlated features (lag1, lag2, roll7) share credit, so importances of individual lags are unreliable. Think in groups.

## Partial dependence: the code

How does predicted demand change with yesterday's temperature, averaging over everything else?

```{r}
#| output: false
grid <- seq(min(tr$temp_l1), max(tr$temp_l1), length.out = 40)
pdp <- sapply(grid, function(v) { d <- te[, xs]; d$temp_l1 <- v;
                                   mean(predict(rf, d)$predictions) })
p_pdp <- tibble(temp = grid, demand = pdp) |>
  ggplot(aes(temp, demand)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Yesterday's maximum temperature (C)", y = "Average predicted demand")
```

- Partial dependence describes the *model*, not causality, and can mislead when features are strongly correlated.

## Partial dependence: learning the U-shape

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_pdp
```

- The forest was never told the relationship is nonlinear. It rises in the cold and, more strongly, in the heat.
- The overall effect is modest (a few GWh): yesterday's demand already carries most of the information.

# 2.11 Global models

## Many series, one model

Data: `tourism`, quarterly trips by region, state and purpose of travel: **304 series**, 80 quarters each (1998-2017).

```{r}
tz <- tourism |> as_tibble() |> mutate(sid = paste(Region, State, Purpose, sep = "|"))
c(series = n_distinct(tz$sid), quarters = n_distinct(tz$Quarter))

wide <- tz |> dplyr::select(sid, Quarter, Trips) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Quarter, values_from = Trips)
M <- as.matrix(wide[, -1]); rownames(M) <- wide$sid
meta <- tz |> distinct(sid, State, Purpose)
dim(M)
```

Plan: hold out the **last 8 quarters of every series** (the same calendar dates for all), forecast 1 to 8 quarters ahead, and compare:

- **Local ETS**, one per series.
- **Local XGBoost**, one per series per horizon (each sees only ~70 rows).
- **Global XGBoost**, one model per horizon trained on all series together.
- Seasonal naive.

## Preparing the global data

```{r}
H <- 8; P <- 8                       # horizon, number of lags
Tn <- ncol(M); Tcut <- Tn - H        # forecast origin: the end of training

scale_i <- rowMeans(M[, 1:Tcut])     # per-series scale, from TRAINING data only
Ms <- M / scale_i                    # every series now has mean about 1

state_code <- as.integer(factor(meta$State[match(rownames(M), meta$sid)]))
purp_code  <- as.integer(factor(meta$Purpose[match(rownames(M), meta$sid)]))
sd_i       <- apply(Ms[, 1:Tcut], 1, sd)          # how volatile is this series?
qtr        <- (seq_len(Tn) - 1) %% 4 + 1          # quarter of the year

feat_at <- function(i, t) c(Ms[i, t:(t - P + 1)], q = qtr[t],
                            state = state_code[i], purp = purp_code[i], sd = sd_i[i])
fnames <- c(paste0("l", 0:(P - 1)), "q", "state", "purp", "sd")
```

- **Normalization** puts big and small series on a common scale so one model can learn shared shapes.
- **Series descriptors** (state, purpose, volatility) let the model treat series differently when it needs to.
- The scale and the volatility are computed from the training period only.

## Training the global and local models

```{r}
fit_xgb_g <- function(X, y) xgb.train(
  params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = 0.05, max_depth = 4,
                subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8),
  data = xgb.DMatrix(X, label = y), nrounds = 300, verbose = 0)

# global: one model per horizon, trained on every series' history
global_models <- lapply(1:H, function(h) {
  rows <- expand.grid(i = seq_len(nrow(M)), t = P:(Tcut - h))
  X <- t(mapply(feat_at, rows$i, rows$t)); colnames(X) <- fnames
  fit_xgb_g(X, Ms[cbind(rows$i, rows$t + h)])
})

origin_X <- t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(M)), function(i) feat_at(i, Tcut)))
colnames(origin_X) <- fnames
pred_global <- sapply(1:H, function(h) predict(global_models[[h]], xgb.DMatrix(origin_X)))
```

```{r}

# local: a separate model for each series and horizon, using only that series' ~70 rows
pred_local <- matrix(NA, nrow(M), H)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(M))) for (h in 1:H) {
  tt <- P:(Tcut - h)
  X <- t(sapply(tt, function(t) feat_at(i, t))); colnames(X) <- fnames
  pred_local[i, h] <- predict(fit_xgb_g(X, Ms[i, tt + h]),
                              xgb.DMatrix(origin_X[i, , drop = FALSE]))
}
```

## Global vs local: what to notice

- **Only the training data differs.** Same features, same settings. The global model for $h = 1$ learns from `r format(nrow(M) * (Tcut - P), big.mark = ",")` rows (`r nrow(M)` series × `r Tcut - P` time points). Each local model sees one series: `r Tcut - P - H + 1` to `r Tcut - P` rows.
- **State, purpose and volatility do nothing locally.** They are constant within a series, so a local model cannot split on them. They let the global model tell series apart.
- **One model per horizon:** `r H` global models, against `r format(nrow(M) * H, big.mark = ",")` local models.

## Scoring: MASE

**MASE** (mean absolute scaled error) divides each series' error by the in-sample seasonal-naive error, making errors comparable across series. Below 1 beats in-sample seasonal naive.

```{r}
actual   <- Ms[, (Tcut + 1):Tn]
mase_den <- apply(Ms[, 1:Tcut], 1, function(v) mean(abs(diff(v, lag = 4))))
mase     <- function(pred) mean(abs(actual - pred) / mase_den)

pred_snaive <- t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(M)), function(i) Ms[i, Tcut - 4 + ((1:H - 1) %% 4) + 1]))

ets_fit <- tz |> filter(Quarter <= sort(unique(tz$Quarter))[Tcut]) |>
  as_tsibble(key = c(Region, State, Purpose, sid), index = Quarter) |>
  model(ETS(Trips))
ets_fc <- ets_fit |> forecast(h = H) |> as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::select(sid, Quarter, .mean) |> pivot_wider(names_from = Quarter, values_from = .mean)
pred_ets <- as.matrix(ets_fc[, -1])[match(rownames(M), ets_fc$sid), ] / scale_i

tibble(model = c("Seasonal naive", "Local XGBoost", "Global XGBoost", "Local ETS"),
       MASE = c(mase(pred_snaive), mase(pred_local), mase(pred_global), mase(pred_ets))) |>
  arrange(MASE) |> mutate(MASE = round(MASE, 3))
```

## What to take from the tourism result

- The **global** XGBoost model does better than the **local** one trained on each series alone: sharing information across series helps when each series is short.
- Both ML models beat seasonal naive.
- **Local ETS is hard to beat here.** Tourism series are smooth, strongly seasonal and short, which is exactly what ETS is built for.
- The global model was given little: no tuning and basic features. Competition-winning global models use richer features and ensembles.
- Bottom line: global models are a good bet with **many** related series, and are not a replacement for a strong classical method on well-behaved seasonal data.

## Design decisions for global models

- **Normalize** each series (by its mean or recent level) and forecast the scaled value, then rescale.
- **Series identifiers or descriptors** as features (category codes, size, volatility); more flexible models can use learned embeddings.
- **Cut every series at the same date** for validation. Training on series A's future while testing on series B's past leaks shared shocks (for example a pandemic).
- **Windows from all series, all times:** the training table is (series × time points) rows, so global models get big quickly.
- **New series with no history (cold start):** global models can forecast from descriptors alone, which local models cannot.
- **Loss and weighting:** an unweighted squared error is dominated by large series, which is why we scaled. Check that errors are fair across series sizes.

# 2.12 Attention and Transformers

## The problem attention solves

- **Fixed window models** (AR, trees on lags) see only the $p$ lags you chose. A relevant event outside the window is invisible.
- **RNN/LSTM** squeeze the past through a bottleneck, one step at a time. Distant events must survive many updates, and training cannot be parallelized across time steps.
- **Attention** connects every time step directly to every other: any past moment can influence the forecast in one step, and the strength of the influence is learned.

## A first look: attention without any learning

Before the Transformer machinery, here is the *idea* in a few lines. To forecast the next sunspot value:

1. Take the last 9 values (the **query**).
2. Compare them with every past window of 9 values (the **keys**).
3. Each past window has a **value**: what came next.
4. Weight the values by how similar the window is to the query, and average.

$$
\hat y_{t+1} = \sum_s w_s\, v_s, \qquad
w_s=\frac{\exp(-\|q-k_s\|^2/\tau)}{\sum_{u}\exp(-\|q-k_u\|^2/\tau)}.
$$

This is "analog forecasting" or a kernel smoother. It has no learned parameters except the temperature $\tau$.

## Attention-style forecasting on sunspots

```{r}
ys <- as.numeric(sqrt(sunspot.year)); yrs <- as.numeric(time(sunspot.year)); pw <- 9
analog <- function(t, tau) {                  # forecast ys[t+1] from windows that end before t
  q <- ys[(t - pw + 1):t]                     # query
  s <- pw:(t - 1)
  K <- t(sapply(s, function(k) ys[(k - pw + 1):k]))   # keys: past windows
  v <- ys[s + 1]                              # values: what came next
  d2 <- rowSums((K - matrix(q, nrow(K), pw, byrow = TRUE))^2)
  w <- exp(-(d2 - min(d2)) / tau); w <- w / sum(w)    # softmax over -distance
  c(pred = sum(w * v), eff_n = 1 / sum(w^2))
}

# choose tau on a validation slice INSIDE the training period (1930-1958)
val <- which(yrs >= 1930 & yrs <= 1957)
sapply(c(1, 5, 20, 100), function(tau)
  c(tau = tau, val_rmse = rmse(ys[val + 1], sapply(val, function(t) analog(t, tau)["pred"]))))
```

## Test results

```{r}
test_t <- which(yrs >= 1959)
tau_sel <- 5                                   # best value on the validation slice
an <- t(sapply(test_t - 1, function(t) analog(t, tau_sel)))

ar9 <- ar(ys[1:which(yrs == 1958)], order.max = 9, aic = FALSE, method = "ols")
ar_pred <- sapply(test_t, function(t) ar9$x.intercept + sum(ar9$ar * ys[(t - 1):(t - 9)]))

c(attention_style = rmse(ys[test_t], an[, "pred"]),
  AR9 = rmse(ys[test_t], ar_pred),
  naive = rmse(ys[test_t], ys[test_t - 1]),
  effective_windows_used = mean(an[, "eff_n"]))
```

- The forecast leans on about `r round(mean(an[, "eff_n"]), 1)` past windows out of hundreds: it **selects** relevant history.
- AR(9) applies the same 9 weights every time. Attention-style weights change with every query.
- This is a toy (one series, nothing learned but $\tau$), but it shows the idea.

## Scaled dot-product attention

A Transformer learns what to compare. For a sequence of $L$ time steps with embeddings $X\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}$:

$$
Q = XW_Q,\quad K = XW_K,\quad V = XW_V,
\qquad
\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)V .
$$

- $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ are **learned** projection matrices.
- $QK^\top$ is an $L\times L$ table of similarity scores: step $i$'s query against step $j$'s key.
- Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the scores from growing with dimension and saturating the softmax.
- Each row of the softmax sums to 1: the weights over the past for that step.
- The output at each step is a weighted average of the **values**.

## One attention head, computed by hand

Six time steps of standardized sunspot values, with random (untrained) projection matrices, to show the mechanics.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
x <- as.numeric(scale(ys[100:105])); L <- length(x); d <- 4
X  <- cbind(x, sin(1:L), cos(1:L), 1)                       # a small "embedding" per step
Wq <- matrix(rnorm(d * d), d); Wk <- matrix(rnorm(d * d), d); Wv <- matrix(rnorm(d * d), d)
Q <- X %*% Wq; K <- X %*% Wk; V <- X %*% Wv

scores <- Q %*% t(K) / sqrt(d)
softmax_rows <- function(S) t(apply(S, 1, function(r) exp(r - max(r)) / sum(exp(r - max(r)))))
A <- softmax_rows(scores)
round(A, 2)
rowSums(A)
```

Row $i$ shows how much step $i$ attends to each step $j$. Here every step can see the future, which is wrong for forecasting. The fix is a mask.

## Causal masking

For forecasting, step $i$ must only attend to steps $j\le i$. Add $-\infty$ to the forbidden scores before the softmax:

```{r}
mask <- matrix(0, L, L); mask[upper.tri(mask)] <- -Inf
A_causal <- softmax_rows(scores + mask)
round(A_causal, 2)
```

- The upper triangle is zero: no looking ahead.
- Without the mask the model could copy the answer from the future, which is leakage inside the architecture.
- Output for step $i$: `A_causal[i, ] %*% V`.

## Order information: positional encoding

Attention treats its inputs as an unordered **set**: shuffle the time steps and the same weights come out (just shuffled). Time order must be injected, for example with sinusoidal encodings:

$$
\text{PE}(pos,2i)=\sin\!\Big(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\Big),\qquad
\text{PE}(pos,2i+1)=\cos\!\Big(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\Big),
$$

added to each step's embedding. Learned position embeddings are an alternative.

## Positional encoding: what it looks like

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
d_model <- 32
pe <- outer(0:23, 0:(d_model - 1),
            function(pos, j) ifelse(j %% 2 == 0, sin(pos / 10000^(j / d_model)),
                                    cos(pos / 10000^((j - 1) / d_model))))
image(t(pe[24:1, ]), axes = FALSE, col = hcl.colors(30, "Blue-Red 3"),
      xlab = "encoding dimension", ylab = "time step (position)")
```

Each row is one time step. Each column is one sine or cosine of a different frequency.

## The Transformer block

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false}, 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    I[Input series: windows or patches] --> E[Embed + add positional encoding]
    E --> A[Multi-head causal self-attention, then add + normalize]
    E -. residual connection .-> A
    A --> F[Feed-forward network on each step, then add + normalize]
    A -. residual connection .-> F
    F --> O[Repeat for N blocks, then output layer: forecast]
```

## The Transformer block: the parts

- **Multi-head:** run several attention heads with different $W_Q,W_K,W_V$ in parallel (each can focus on a different pattern, e.g. recent steps, same weekday last week) and concatenate.
- **Residual connections and normalization** make deep stacks trainable.
- **Cost:** the score table is $L\times L$, so memory and time grow like $L^2$ in the sequence length.
- The same block, stacked, is the basis of language models, and has been adapted to forecasting.

## Transformers for time series: what to know

- Applying language-model machinery directly to time points can work poorly: a single time step carries little information (unlike a word), and attention over individual points can blur temporal order.
- A well-known study, Zeng et al. (2023), reported that very simple linear models outperformed several Transformer forecasters on standard benchmarks. The lesson: **compare to simple baselines**.
- A common remedy, **patching** (for example PatchTST): group consecutive points into patches and treat each patch as a token, so attention works on meaningful chunks and the sequence is shorter.
- Strengths in practice: long inputs, many series trained together, multivariate dependence.
- Costs: data hunger, tuning, compute, and less interpretability than ETS or ARIMA.

## Attention vs the models you know

| Model | How weights on the past are determined |
|---|---|
| AR($p$) | Fixed coefficients on $p$ lags, same for every forecast |
| Exponential smoothing | Fixed geometric decay on the past |
| Trees on lags | Rules on a chosen set of lag features |
| RNN / LSTM | Compressed into a running state, gated by learned rules |
| Attention | Weights recomputed from the content of the current context |

AR and exponential smoothing are special cases of "weighted average of the past" with weights frozen in advance. Attention lets the weights respond.

# 2.13 Putting it together

## Failure modes at a glance

| Method | Typical failure | Warning sign | Remedy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trees on lags | Cannot extrapolate trends | Forecasts flatten at the training maximum | Difference the target; hybrid with a trend model |
| Trees on lags | Leakage via rolling features or shuffled CV | Test error much better than seems plausible | Strict time ordering; compute features from the past only |
| Boosting | Overfitting with many rounds | Training error falls, validation error rises | Early stopping on a later validation period; smaller `eta` |
| Random forest | Optimistic OOB error | OOB much better than time-ordered CV | Time-ordered validation |
| Global models | Series on different scales; leakage across series | Large series dominate; surprisingly good test scores | Normalize; cut all series at the same date |
| Attention / Transformers | Overfit small data; losing temporal order | Linear or seasonal-naive baselines are competitive | Baselines first; patching; more data |
| Everything | One split, one seed | Rankings change when you re-run | Rolling origins, several seeds, report spread |

## A practical workflow

1. Plot the data. Identify trend, seasonality, calendar effects, number of series.
2. Fit simple baselines (seasonal naive, ETS, ARIMA). Record their time-ordered holdout errors.
3. Build lag, rolling and calendar features using only the past. Check for leakage.
4. Try a random forest as a robust first ML model; then boosting with early stopping on a later validation period.
5. Handle trends explicitly (differencing or a hybrid).
6. If you have many related series, try a global model with normalization and descriptors.
7. Compare against the baselines on **held-out, time-ordered** data, over more than one origin.
8. Add uncertainty (quantile model or conformal), and check coverage.
9. Consider attention-based or other deep models only when you have lots of data and a reason, and benchmark them against steps 2 to 6.

## Results on these slides, in one place

- **Electricity (one series, calendar and temperature):** XGBoost beat plain ARIMA, but ETS and a lag regression with the same calendar information were better; tuning did not help on the test year.
- **Trending series:** tree models on levels failed badly; differencing the target repaired most of the damage, but classical models extrapolated best.
- **Multi-step (sunspots):** neither direct nor recursive won consistently; the winner changed by horizon.
- **Tourism (304 series):** global beat local ML, but local ETS was best.
- **Attention-style toy (sunspots):** selective lookback beat a fixed-weight AR(9) on this series.

Take-away: machine learning methods are strong additions to the toolbox, not replacements for it.

## Self-check: Part 2

1. Why is shuffled $k$-fold CV inappropriate for time series? What replaces it?
2. A teammate computes a 7-day rolling mean of demand including today and uses it as a feature. What is wrong?
3. Explain why a random forest cannot predict above the highest value in its training data. Name two fixes.
4. In boosting with squared error, what does each new tree fit?
5. What happens to a forest's variance as you add trees? As you lower `mtry`?
6. When would you prefer a direct to a recursive multi-step strategy?
7. Why normalize each series before training a global model?
8. What do the $Q$, $K$, $V$ matrices represent, and what does the $\sqrt{d_k}$ do?
9. Why does forecasting need a causal mask, and what does positional encoding add?
10. What did our tourism and electricity results show about ML versus classical methods?

## Answers: Part 2

1. It trains on the future of test rows and splits near-duplicate neighbouring rows across folds. Use rolling-origin (expanding window) validation with training always before testing.
2. The window includes the target day, so the feature contains the answer. Compute the mean from lagged values only, then roll.
3. Each leaf predicts an average of training targets, so predictions lie within the training range. Fixes: model differences or growth rates; fit a trend first and use trees on the residuals (also linear trees, or normalization).
4. The residuals of the current ensemble (the negative gradient of squared error), scaled by the learning rate when added.
5. Variance falls toward the floor $\rho\sigma^2$ as trees are added. Lowering `mtry` lowers the correlation $\rho$ between trees, which lowers that floor, at the cost of weaker individual trees.
6. When errors compounding through recursion are a concern, or when later-horizon forecasts would need unavailable future inputs; direct trains each horizon on its own target.
7. So that large and small series are on a common scale and the loss is not dominated by large series; shapes become shareable.
8. Queries ask "what am I looking for", keys say "what do I contain", values hold the content to be mixed. $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the dot products from growing with dimension, which would push the softmax into saturation.
9. Without the mask a step could attend to the future (leakage). Attention is order-blind, so positional encoding supplies time order.
10. ML methods are competitive and shine with many predictors or many series, but are not automatically better; well-specified classical models (ETS on tourism, trend models) remained very strong, and results depend on the data.

## Further reading

- Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: Principles and Practice* (3rd ed.), for the classical baselines used here.
- Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*: trees, bagging, random forests, boosting.
- Breiman (2001), "Random Forests"; Chen and Guestrin (2016), "XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System".
- Vaswani et al. (2017), "Attention Is All You Need".
- Zeng et al. (2023), "Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?"; Nie et al. (2023), PatchTST.
- Makridakis et al. on the M5 competition (gradient boosting and global models featured prominently in the top entries).
